description: Classical number-theoretic and combinatorial techniques — sieves, modular arithmetic, GCD, combinatorics, randomized sampling, geometry, and search-space splitting — that appear as the unlocking subroutine inside harder OA and interview problems rather than as problems in their own right.
important_details: The Sieve of Eratosthenes precomputes primality across a whole range in O(n log log n); trial division per query is O(sqrt(n)) each and does not scale.
Fast exponentiation computes a^b mod m in O(log b) by squaring the base and halving the exponent.
Under a modulus you cannot divide directly — you multiply by the modular inverse, obtained via Fermat's Little Theorem when the modulus is prime.
Meet in the Middle splits a 2^n search space into two 2^(n/2) halves, which is the standard rescue when n sits around 30 to 40.
Overflow is the silent killer in this pattern: use long for intermediate products and take the modulus after every multiplication.
other_relevant_details: These techniques rarely form the whole question. Recognize them from constraints: 'answer modulo 1e9+7' implies modular arithmetic and possibly modular inverses; 'primes/divisors up to N' implies a sieve; n around 30-40 implies meet in the middle; 'random pick with unknown stream length' implies reservoir sampling. Learning to spot the constraint-to-technique mapping is worth more than memorizing any single algorithm here.

variations.description: Precompute primality for every number up to N by iteratively marking multiples of each discovered prime as composite.
important_details: Start marking from p*p rather than 2*p, since all smaller multiples were already marked by smaller primes.
The outer loop only needs to run while p*p <= n; cast to long in that comparison to avoid overflow for large n.
Once built, primality is an O(1) array lookup for any value up to N.
A segmented sieve handles ranges too large for memory by sieving fixed-size blocks using the primes up to sqrt(high).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log log n). Space: O(n).

problems.name: Find the Count of Numbers Which Are Not Special

variations.description: Factor numbers efficiently either by trial division up to sqrt(n) for a single value, or by precomputing the smallest prime factor for every number up to N so any factorization takes O(log n).
important_details: Trial division only needs to test up to sqrt(n); after the loop, any remaining value greater than 1 is itself a prime factor.
The SPF sieve stores each number's smallest prime factor during a modified sieve pass, then factorization is repeated division by spf[x].
Divisor counting follows from the exponents: if n = p1^a * p2^b, the divisor count is (a+1)(b+1).
Divisors come in pairs around sqrt(n), so enumerating divisors also costs only O(sqrt(n)).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(sqrt(n)) per number by trial division, O(log n) per number after an O(n log log n) SPF sieve. Space: O(n) for the SPF table.

problems.name: Largest Component Size by Common Factor
Distinct Prime Factors of Product of Array
Minimize the Maximum of Two Arrays

variations.description: Compute a^b, optionally modulo m, in O(log b) by repeated squaring — multiply the accumulator whenever the current exponent bit is set, then square the base and shift.
important_details: Take the modulus after every multiplication and use long arithmetic, or you overflow silently on 32-bit ints.
Reduce the base modulo m before the loop starts to keep intermediate values small.
For negative exponents (as in pow(x, n) with n < 0), compute the positive power and invert; guard against Integer.MIN_VALUE, whose negation overflows.
This is the engine behind modular inverses and therefore behind any nCr-mod-p computation.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log b). Space: O(1) iterative.

problems.name: Number of Ways to Stay in the Same Place After Some Steps

variations.description: Compute greatest common divisors via repeated remainder, derive LCM from it, and use both for fraction reduction, cycle alignment, and grid-lattice problems.
important_details: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) with base case gcd(a, 0) = a, running in O(log(min(a,b))).
lcm(a, b) = (a / gcd(a,b)) * b — divide BEFORE multiplying to avoid overflow.
The extended Euclidean algorithm additionally returns coefficients x, y with ax + by = gcd(a,b), which gives modular inverses for non-prime moduli.
A linear Diophantine equation ax + by = c has integer solutions exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c — this single fact solves the water-jug problem outright.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log(min(a,b))). Space: O(1) iterative.

problems.name: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array

variations.description: Compute binomial coefficients, permutations, and Catalan numbers under a prime modulus by precomputing factorials and their modular inverses via Fermat's Little Theorem.
important_details: Fermat's Little Theorem: for prime p, the inverse of a is a^(p-2) mod p, computed with fast exponentiation.
Precompute factorial[i] and invFactorial[i] up to the maximum n once, then every nCr query is O(1).
Build the inverse factorial array backwards from invFactorial[n] using invFactorial[i-1] = invFactorial[i] * i, which costs one exponentiation total rather than n.
Catalan(n) = C(2n, n) / (n+1) counts balanced-parenthesis strings, distinct BSTs, and valid triangulations — recognize these shapes.
For a non-prime modulus, Fermat does not apply; use the extended Euclidean algorithm instead.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) precomputation, O(1) per query. Space: O(n).

problems.name: Number of Ways to Reorder Array to Get Same BST

variations.description: Operate on a number's decimal or arbitrary-base digits directly — extracting, reversing, summing, or converting — without string conversion, watching carefully for overflow.
important_details: Extract digits with n % base and n /= base; this naturally produces them least-significant first.
Reversing an integer overflows easily: check result > (Integer.MAX_VALUE - digit) / 10 BEFORE the multiplication, not after.
Palindrome checks on integers can avoid string conversion by reversing only the second half and comparing.
Digit DP (counting numbers with a digit property up to N) builds on this and pairs with memoization over position, tightness, and accumulated state.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(number of digits) = O(log n). Space: O(1).

variations.description: Select k items uniformly at random from a stream of unknown length in a single pass using O(k) memory, replacing a held item with probability k/i at the i-th element.
important_details: Algorithm R: keep the first k items; for each subsequent item i (1-indexed), pick j uniformly in [0, i) and replace reservoir[j] if j < k.
The uniformity proof is an induction showing every seen item retains probability k/n of being in the reservoir at any point.
For k = 1 the rule simplifies to: replace the held item with probability 1/i — this is the linked-list random-node problem.
Essential when the stream length is unknown or too large to store, which is exactly how these problems are phrased.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) single pass. Space: O(k), independent of the stream length.

variations.description: Split an exponential search space into two halves, brute-force each half at 2^(n/2) cost, then combine the halves with sorting plus binary search or a hash map.
important_details: Reduces O(2^n) to roughly O(2^(n/2) * n), which is the difference between infeasible and instant for n around 40.
Standard shape: enumerate all subset sums of each half, sort one side, then binary search each value from the other side for its complement.
The combination step must be efficient (log or constant per item), or you have simply relocated the exponential cost.
Memory is the real constraint — 2^20 entries is about a million longs, which is fine, but 2^25 is not.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(2^(n/2) * n). Space: O(2^(n/2)).

problems.name: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference
Ways to Split Array Into Good Subarrays

variations.description: Handle points, lines, slopes, areas, and overlaps using exact integer arithmetic wherever possible to avoid floating-point precision failures.
important_details: Compare slopes as cross products (dy1 * dx2 == dy2 * dx1) rather than dividing — this keeps everything in integers and avoids division by zero.
The cross product's sign gives orientation (clockwise, counter-clockwise, collinear), which is the primitive behind convex hull and segment intersection.
Compare squared distances instead of distances to skip the square root entirely.
Rectangle overlap is easiest as its negation: two rectangles do NOT overlap if one is entirely left, right, above, or below the other.
For collinear-points problems, normalize slope fractions by their GCD and keep the sign in a consistent position before hashing them.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n^2) for pairwise slope problems. Space: O(n).

variations.description: Defensive numerical technique: detect or prevent overflow before it happens, handle Integer.MIN_VALUE asymmetry, and choose safe idioms for midpoints, negation, and accumulation.
important_details: Compute midpoints as low + (high - low) / 2, never (low + high) / 2, which overflows for large indices.
Integer.MIN_VALUE has no positive counterpart: Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) returns itself, and negating it overflows. Cast to long first.
Check before multiplying: if (result > LIMIT / factor) it will overflow — checking after the fact reads a corrupted value.
Java silently wraps on integer overflow rather than throwing, so these bugs pass small tests and fail on the judge's large cases.
Prefer long for accumulators such as running sums and products whenever the constraints allow values near 10^9.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1). These checks cost nothing asymptotically and prevent an entire class of judge failures.
